title: Words That Build: Speaking Truth in Love

paragraphs.text: Before you begin
Moses Afolabi • Illustrated study edition • 2026
Read each Bible passage in context. Quotations use the King James Version. Modern scenes are fictional teaching examples. Historical reflections include source links.
This independently written edition does not reproduce an IDPLR supplier manuscript or artwork. It does not assert supplier modification or byline permissions.
Use a notebook for the practical exercises. Study each visual summary, try a suitable action, and review what happened. Discuss difficult questions with a trusted pastor or mature believer.
The PDF has still illustrations. The separate companion adds gentle motion and reflection prompts.

Chapter 1 Give Your Words a Useful Purpose
Give a message a clear purpose that serves the people receiving it.
Read Ephesians 4:25–32, Colossians 4:2–6, and Proverbs 12:18.
Begin with the person who will hear
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers. — Ephesians 4:29, KJV

Paul asks believers to consider the effect of their words upon those who hear. Read the verse within the call to truth, responsible anger, useful work, kindness, and forgiveness. Speech belongs to the life believers share. The aim reaches beyond sounding pleasant. A necessary correction, a clear instruction, and a truthful encouragement can each help a hearer in a different way.

Before speaking, ask what the message needs to accomplish. Are you giving information, asking a question, requesting an action, correcting a mistake, or offering comfort? A message becomes confusing when it tries to perform several hidden tasks at once. A request for help can become a complaint about loyalty before the other person understands what is being asked.
This book's particular task

Listening is essential to communication, and the companion title Listen First treats that skill in depth. This book concentrates on forming the message you will speak or write. You will examine its purpose, accuracy, clarity, manner, audience, and follow-through. Receiving an account carefully and preparing a useful response support one another, but they are distinct tasks.

Choose a real responsibility for practice. It may involve family arrangements, ministry teamwork, study, customer service, or an ordinary workplace. Keep private information secure as you use the exercises. You can alter identifying details in a personal example or work with one of the clearly fictional situations in the book.
Biblical picture · A word can injure or help
There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health. — Proverbs 12:18, KJV

The proverb uses a powerful comparison to describe speech. It invites examination of words that wound carelessly and words offered with wisdom. Read it as wisdom about conduct, rather than as a guarantee that a sentence cures an illness. Ask what the hearer actually needs from your message and whether its wording serves that need.

A correction should identify what must change. Comfort should give room to a person's actual sorrow. A request should make the action and its timing understandable. Those purposes require different words. A gentle manner helps, and so does the courage to state a difficult fact plainly where that fact must be addressed.
A worked request with a hidden complaint

Imagine a fictional coordinator in Singapore who writes, “If anyone cared about this team, the room would be ready.” The sentence expresses frustration but does not identify who should do what or when. Several people assume it concerns someone else. Another person feels accused despite having completed the task assigned to them.

The coordinator rewrites it as, “Could you arrange the twelve chairs before the group arrives at six? Please tell me by four if you need help.” The new message names the action, the deadline, and a way to report a difficulty. If there is also a recurring fairness concern, it belongs in a separate conversation with the people responsible. Clarity prevents that concern from being hidden inside a general accusation.
Let love examine the message's motive

Sometimes the stated purpose differs from the desired effect. You may say you are giving information while hoping to embarrass a colleague. You may describe a question as concern while using it to spread suspicion. Bring that motive honestly before God. Ask which facts must be communicated and which details mainly serve the wish to injure.

Colossians 4:6 connects gracious speech with knowing how to answer each person. A particular hearer and situation require attention. A public announcement may need brevity and clear action. A sensitive personal matter may need a private setting and time for questions. Choose the form that fits the responsibility, rather than the audience that gives your frustration the most attention.
Visual summary
Identify the hearer’s need
Choose one useful purpose
Form a message that serves
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Prepare one purposeful message

Write the message's job in one sentence. Then draft the opening, the necessary facts, and the action or response being invited. Read it as the recipient might encounter it. Could they identify what they need to know and what they are being asked to do? Remove a hidden accusation or an unnecessary demand. Keep the message truthful, useful, and proportionate to its purpose.
Prayer. Father, help my words serve the people who hear them. Give me truth, clarity, and love in the particular message I need to prepare today. Amen.
Chapter 2 Say What You Know, and Mark What You Do Not
Check the record and distinguish a known fact from an assumption.
Read Ephesians 4:25, Proverbs 18:13–17, and Luke 1:1–4.
Truth belongs to a shared life
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another. — Ephesians 4:25, KJV

Paul links truthful speech with belonging to one another. An inaccurate statement can influence how people treat a colleague, plan work, or understand a family member. Accuracy is therefore a form of care. Ask which part of your account you observed, which part came from another person, and which part is an interpretation you have supplied.

Those distinctions can be stated simply. “I saw the file arrive at ten” differs from “I was told it arrived at ten.” “The reply has not reached me” differs from “She has refused to answer.” A missing reply may have several explanations. Keep an unanswered question open until you have information that can responsibly close it.
Hear another account before making a conclusion public
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. — Proverbs 18:17, KJV

The proverb warns against the appearance of completeness in a single account. It does not require treating every claim as equally reliable. It calls for care before reaching a verdict. Ask what information is missing, who may have relevant knowledge, and which question could clarify the matter without spreading it unnecessarily.

Where immediate safety or a serious report is involved, use an appropriate responsible channel promptly. You do not need to conduct your own private investigation before seeking qualified help. For ordinary misunderstandings, a direct factual question may resolve the issue. Match the inquiry to the responsibility and avoid turning uncertainty into an invitation for a wider audience to speculate.
Biblical testimony · Luke explains his account

Read Luke 1:1–4. Luke refers to accounts, eyewitnesses, careful understanding, and an orderly presentation to Theophilus. The opening helps the reader recognize that the message has a stated purpose and an account of how it is being presented. Read it within the Gospel's witness to Jesus, rather than reducing it to a generic modern reporting manual.

Its attention to an orderly account can still question our careless certainty. If you present a claim to someone, explain the information needed for them to understand it responsibly. Do not describe a secondhand story as your own observation or imply that you checked a detail you have never examined.
A worked correction of an assumption

Imagine a fictional team member in Birmingham who tells a supervisor that a colleague ignored a request. The member has sent one email and received no reply. Before repeating the accusation, he checks the address and discovers that the message went to an old account. He then corrects his statement with the supervisor and sends the request through the current channel.

His correction names both the inaccurate claim and the new fact. “I said she ignored the request. I had used the wrong address and do not know whether she received it” is clear. It avoids leaving the colleague under a suspicion that the speaker now knows is unsupported. If another person heard the first account, that person also needs an appropriate correction.
Handle numbers, quotations, and examples carefully

A number can give a message an appearance of precision. State where it comes from and what it actually counts. Twelve responses are not necessarily twelve satisfied customers. A quotation should represent the speaker's words and retain enough context to preserve its meaning. A shortened quotation should not remove the sentence that changes the point.

Label an invented example as fictional. When using a historical account, consult a reliable source and distinguish the record from your application. Scripture should be quoted accurately and explained in context. These practices help a reader assess the claim without having to discover later that the most confident part of the message was imagined.
Visual summary
Check what is known
Mark what remains uncertain
Correct unsupported claims
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Check one claim before you repeat it

Choose a statement in a message you are preparing. Write its source, the part you verified, and the uncertainty that remains. Ask whether the recipient needs the full detail or a concise statement with a source they can consult. Correct a claim that exceeds the evidence. If the information is unnecessary to the message's purpose, consider leaving it out rather than circulating it merely because it is interesting.
Prayer. Lord, make me careful with truth. Help me distinguish knowledge from assumption, seek the information my responsibility requires, and correct an inaccurate account without delay. Amen.
Chapter 3 Make Requests and Agreements Understandable
A useful agreement identifies the task, the person, and the deadline.
Read Matthew 5:33–37, Colossians 4:5–6, and Acts 15:22–31.
Let a promise have a clear meaning
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. — Matthew 5:37, KJV

Read Jesus' words within His teaching about oaths and truthful speech. The instruction challenges the attempt to create credibility through elaborate declarations while leaving ordinary words unreliable. A clear yes or no should mean something the other person can understand. Avoid accepting a task in language that conceals the fact you have not checked whether you can perform it.

If you need information before agreeing, say so. “I can confirm after checking the timetable at two” is more truthful than an enthusiastic yes followed by silence. A conditional offer should name the condition. “I can prepare the slides if I receive the approved text by Tuesday” tells the requester what the arrangement requires.
Give a request the details needed for action

A useful request identifies the action, the person responsible, the timing, and the expected result. Add the information or support required to perform it. A request to review a document may need to state whether the reader should check facts, spelling, tone, or the final decision. Without that distinction, several people may each do a different task and all believe they have complied.

Ask the recipient to confirm the agreement in their own words when the task is important or unfamiliar. This is a check on shared understanding, not a test intended to embarrass them. If their account differs, clarify the missing part before work begins. The small conversation may prevent a larger correction later.
Biblical testimony · A letter and trusted messengers

Read Acts 15:22–31. The Jerusalem church sends a letter with chosen messengers concerning a particular controversy. The account identifies the audience, the matter addressed, and people who will help communicate the decision. The receiving believers hear the message and respond. Read the instructions within their specific apostolic and historical setting.

The account helps us notice that a message may need both a written record and an opportunity for explanation. A short document can preserve the agreed wording. A responsible person can answer questions about the particular task. Do not assume that sending a message is the same as establishing that the recipient understood it.
A worked agreement about a review

Imagine a fictional ministry leader in Lagos who asks a volunteer to “check the booklet.” The volunteer corrects spelling, while the leader expected a factual review of quotations. They discover the mismatch only when the printing date approaches. For the next task, they agree on three checks, the version to be reviewed, and the date for comments.

The volunteer reports which checks were completed and identifies two quotations requiring further verification. The leader decides who will resolve them before approval. The agreement makes the work and its limits visible. It does not turn the volunteer into the final authority over every aspect of the publication.
Keep a change from disappearing between people

When an agreement changes, tell the people whose work depends on it. State what changed, what remains, and which action is now required. Avoid sending an ambiguous update that assumes everyone remembers the entire earlier conversation. Identify the current version of a document or plan so people do not continue working from different instructions.

If you must withdraw a promise, explain promptly and propose what you can responsibly offer. An apology does not replace the information needed to make another arrangement. Ask whether a partial completion, a later date, or a different person would help. Leave the recipient free to decide which alternative fits their responsibility.
Visual summary
Name the task and owner
Agree on scope and timing
Confirm shared understanding
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Draft and confirm a clear request

Write a real request using the action, expected result, timing, and available support. Remove vague words that hide the decision. Ask the recipient which information is still missing and whether the timing is workable. Record the actual agreement in a form both can find. At the end, review whether the result matched the request and which instruction would be clearer next time.
Prayer. Father, help my yes and no remain truthful. Give me clarity in requests, humility to check understanding, and faithfulness in the agreements I make. Amen.
Chapter 4 Speak Difficult Truth With Care
Describe the specific problem and explain what needs to change.
Read Ephesians 4:11–16, Proverbs 27:5–6, and Galatians 2:11–14.
Keep truth and love in the same purpose
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ: — Ephesians 4:15, KJV

Read the verse within Paul's description of the body growing toward maturity in Christ. Truthful speech serves that growth. It should not become a disguise for unloading contempt. Love should not become a reason for hiding a serious problem that continues to harm people. Ask what the person and the shared responsibility actually need to have addressed.

A useful correction concerns an action that can be described and a change that can be understood. “The figures on these two pages do not agree” opens a factual discussion. “You are careless about everything” moves from a particular error to a verdict about the whole person. The second statement gives little direction for repair and may obscure the issue that needs attention.
Choose the setting that fits the wrong

A private mistake usually does not need a public audience. A public false claim may require a correction reaching those who heard it. Serious harm may need reporting through an appropriate channel rather than a private conversation. Decide the audience from the responsibility, the people affected, and the need for protection or accountability.

Do not promise secrecy where a responsible process requires sharing information. Explain the limit and use the appropriate channel. If a conversation could create danger, seek suitable support and prioritize safety. The call to speak truth does not assign every person the task of confronting every wrong alone.
Biblical testimony · Paul addresses Peter's conduct

In Galatians 2:11–14, Paul recounts confronting Peter concerning conduct affecting the fellowship of Jewish and Gentile believers. The issue concerns the truth of the gospel and a public pattern that influences others. Read Paul's explanation of the event before treating it as permission to criticize any person publicly whenever you feel strongly.

The account shows why the setting and significance of a wrong matter. Some matters require a response proportionate to their public effect. Others require a quiet correction. Ask what responsibility you have, what facts you can establish, and which audience needs the truth. A strong message should remain accountable to its purpose.
A worked feedback conversation

Imagine a fictional supervisor in Cape Town reviewing a report with an employee. Two totals do not match the supporting table. The supervisor opens with the specific discrepancy and asks how the totals were produced. The employee explains that one page contains an older version. They identify the current figures and agree which documents must be corrected.

The supervisor also discusses the review process needed before the next submission. The employee has a chance to ask questions and suggest a check that fits the workflow. The conversation is firm about accuracy and clear about responsibility. It does not require a speech about the employee's character or a performance of humiliation before the correction can begin.
Make feedback usable

Name the event, its effect, and the change being requested. Give an example where the expectation might otherwise remain vague. Ask the person to explain what they understood and which support they need. If you are discussing a recurring pattern, bring representative facts rather than an unexamined always or never.

Proverbs 27:5–6 values faithful correction over a pleasant appearance that conceals a need. Read the verses carefully and examine your own willingness to receive feedback. The person who speaks should also be prepared to correct a mistaken account. Authority does not make your first interpretation infallible.
Visual summary
Describe the specific issue
Explain its practical effect
Ask for a fitting change
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Prepare a correction you could explain afterward

Write the action at issue and the evidence supporting your account. Identify the effect on people or work, then draft a specific request. Choose an appropriate setting and a way to hear the response. Afterward, record the agreement and any fact that changed your understanding. Follow up on the actual correction, rather than treating the difficult conversation itself as the completed task.
Prayer. Lord, give me courage to speak what needs to be said and humility about my own understanding. Let truth and love govern the purpose, manner, and follow-through of my correction. Amen.
Chapter 5 Encourage Without Flattery or False Promises
Truthful encouragement identifies a real contribution and offers fitting support.
Read 1 Thessalonians 5:9–15, Hebrews 10:23–25, and Acts 11:19–26.
Give encouragement something true to stand on
Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do. — 1 Thessalonians 5:11, KJV

Paul's instruction follows his teaching about the salvation and life believers have through Christ. Encouragement can rest on what God has revealed and on a truthful account of a person's conduct. It does not require predicting an outcome you cannot know. “Christ has received those who trust Him” differs from “You will certainly receive the job tomorrow.” One rests on the gospel; the other may be an invented assurance.

Ask what would help the person continue faithfully in the responsibility before them. They may need recognition of a useful contribution, a reminder of a biblical promise, or a practical offer of assistance. Encouragement is stronger when its words correspond to the actual need and the truth you are able to speak.
Describe the action and its effect

Specific recognition can help someone understand what was useful. “Your clear handover helped me complete the visit without another call” names an action and an effect. “You are the only person who ever helps” may sound generous while unfairly dismissing others and placing an expanding burden on the recipient.

Avoid praise that secretly demands more work. Thank the person for what they did, then make a separate request if another task needs discussion. Give them room to explain the cost of a recurring responsibility. Their faithful contribution may need support or a different arrangement rather than another compliment about managing alone.
Biblical testimony · Barnabas sees grace and exhorts

Read Acts 11:19–26. Barnabas comes to Antioch, sees the grace of God, rejoices, and encourages the believers to continue with the Lord. He also seeks Saul, and they teach among the believers. The account joins recognition, encouragement, and practical contribution to their growth.

The object of his exhortation matters. He directs people toward the Lord, rather than making himself the center of their confidence. A Christian encourager can ask whether the words help another person understand and respond to Christ. Useful support may include time spent teaching or sharing work, rather than only an inspiring sentence.
A worked word to an overlooked volunteer

Imagine a fictional church member in Vancouver noticing a volunteer who quietly prepares the room each week. She thanks him for a particular morning when the clear arrangement helped a newcomer find a place. Then she asks how the responsibility is going. He explains that the new starting time has made preparation difficult.

She does not answer with another speech about his dedication. With his agreement, she brings the scheduling concern to the responsible coordinator and offers one suitable task she can carry. The encouragement has named real good and led into a useful response. The volunteer remains free to discuss a change without feeling that gratitude has trapped him in the role.
Let comfort leave room for sorrow

First Thessalonians 5 also calls for patience, support for the weak, and encouragement for the fainthearted. Read the instructions together. A person can need comfort without being ready to describe the situation positively. Ask whether they would welcome prayer, a passage, quiet company, or a practical offer. Avoid making them protect your enthusiasm by hiding what still hurts.

If you do not know why something happened, say so. You can still speak of God's character from Scripture and keep a concrete promise of support. A short truthful message followed by reliable action may serve the person more faithfully than a confident explanation of a circumstance you do not understand.
Visual summary
Name the real contribution
Explain why it helped
Offer appropriate support
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Prepare one specific encouragement

Choose a person and identify the action, contribution, or biblical truth you can name accurately. Consider whether a private note or a public acknowledgment would be appropriate. Ask permission before sharing a story involving sensitive information. Offer the words without adding a hidden demand. Later, fulfill any practical commitment you made. Let the encouragement remain accountable to truth and love.
Prayer. Father, make my encouragement truthful and useful. Help me recognize Your grace, honor real contributions, and support people without flattery, pressure, or invented promises. Amen.
Chapter 6 Speak Up for What Needs Protection
Bring a concrete concern to the person responsible for addressing it.
Read Proverbs 31:8–9, Ecclesiastes 3:1–8, and Acts 16:35–40.
Understand the responsibility to give voice
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy. — Proverbs 31:8–9, KJV

Read these words within the instruction addressed to a ruler. They concern the use of authority for just judgment and the protection of vulnerable people. A modern application must consider the actual role you hold. You may need to report a concern, support someone in making their own account, or correct an exclusion within your area of responsibility.

Ask the person affected what they want shared where that is possible and appropriate. Do not replace their voice with a dramatic story designed to make yourself appear courageous. Sometimes urgent protection or a required report limits what can remain private. Use the suitable responsible channel and share information proportionate to the purpose.
A time to speak can require preparation

Ecclesiastes 3 includes a time to keep silence and a time to speak. Read the poem as wisdom about varied human circumstances, rather than a command to be silent whenever speech is uncomfortable. Consider the consequences of silence as well as the risks of speaking. A delayed correction may leave someone wrongly blamed or allow a preventable problem to continue.

Prepare the facts you know, the concern they establish, and the action you are requesting. If the matter requires expertise or authority you do not possess, seek the appropriate person. A factual report can state uncertainty without becoming weak. “I heard these words and am concerned about what they may mean” preserves the distinction between observation and conclusion.
Biblical testimony · Paul names a public wrong

Read Acts 16:35–40 with the preceding account of Paul and Silas in Philippi. When officials seek to release them quietly, Paul identifies their Roman citizenship and the public treatment they received. The officials respond to that information. The event concerns a particular historical legal setting, not a statement of present-day rights in every country.

The account challenges the assumption that Christian faith always requires accepting a false public account without response. A person may appropriately identify a wrong through the relevant process. Seek current qualified advice where legal rights or reporting obligations are involved. The practical task is to communicate accurate facts through an appropriate channel, rather than improvise a legal claim from an ancient narrative.
Historical reflection · Douglass addresses his audience directly

On July 5, 1852, Frederick Douglass delivered an address in Rochester challenging the celebration of liberty while slavery continued. The surviving text identifies the people whose suffering the public celebration excluded and presses the audience to face that contradiction. His speech is a particular historical act of moral witness, rather than a script for every disagreement. Frederick Douglass, address of July 5, 1852, The American Presidency Project

The limited lesson concerns refusing to let a comfortable public story erase the people harmed. A message about injustice may need direct, serious language. Examine its accuracy, audience, and purpose. Care for the hearer does not require protecting a falsehood from being challenged.
A worked report about an unsafe arrangement

Imagine a fictional team member in Madrid who notices that a recurring event plan leaves one exit obstructed. She records the location and the times she observed it, then reports the concern to the person responsible for the venue. She asks for confirmation that the arrangement will be checked before the next event. If the danger is immediate, she uses the appropriate urgent process instead of waiting for an ordinary meeting.

Her message does not speculate about who wanted to cause harm. It identifies the condition, the responsibility, and the action needed. She keeps a suitable record of the report and follows up through the relevant channel. The example is about clear communication of a concern; it cannot replace a venue's current safety requirements or qualified assessment.
Visual summary
Identify the concrete concern
Reach a responsible person
Record the needed follow-up
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Prepare a responsible statement

Choose a concern within your role. Write what you observed, who may be affected, what remains uncertain, and which person can act. Ask whether the affected person's privacy or safety changes the channel you should use. Draft a clear request and a suitable follow-up point. Courage and preparation can work together in speech that seeks protection and truth.
Prayer. Lord, give me wisdom about when and how to speak. Help me protect dignity, report truthfully, and use the responsibility I hold for what is just and good. Amen.
Chapter 7 Write Messages People Can Use
Write a clear message with the necessary context and an understandable request.
Read Proverbs 10:19, James 3:1–12, and Ephesians 6:21–24.
Let each sentence serve the message
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise. — Proverbs 10:19, KJV

The proverb commends restraint in speech. It does not require every useful explanation to be short. A complex instruction may need detail. The question is whether the words serve understanding or mainly multiply an impression, accusation, or display. Ask what the recipient needs to know, decide, or do after reading.

Start with the purpose. Put the necessary action or main information early. Group related facts and mark any deadline clearly. If a message needs background, explain why that background matters to the request. A person should not have to read through a long account of your frustration before discovering that they are being asked to confirm a meeting time.
Give the reader a usable structure

A practical message often needs an opening purpose, a few relevant facts, and a clear request or next step. The exact form can vary. For a changed appointment, state the current arrangement, the proposed change, and what response you need. For a document review, identify the version and the particular checks requested.

Use familiar words and explain a necessary technical term. Avoid abbreviations the reader has not been given. If several tasks are involved, number them and say who owns each one. A list is useful when it clarifies parallel actions; it cannot replace explaining what an unfamiliar task means.
Biblical testimony · A trusted messenger gives context

In Ephesians 6:21–22, Paul identifies Tychicus and the purpose of sending him. The believers will receive information about Paul's affairs, and their hearts will be comforted. The closing passage recognizes a person entrusted with communicating context beyond the written letter. Read it within its apostolic setting.

A modern message may also need someone who can explain an arrangement or answer a question. State whom to contact and what that person is responsible for. Do not name someone as the contact without confirming their agreement and ability to help. A clear handoff protects both the reader and the person receiving the next inquiry.
A worked rewrite of an unclear email

Imagine a fictional project assistant in São Paulo drafting a long email about a postponed training session. The opening describes every call made during the week. The new date appears near the end, while the request for confirmation is hidden in a final sentence. Several recipients miss the action.

She rewrites the message to begin with the new date and the confirmation needed by Friday. The next paragraph explains the one change affecting preparation. She identifies the current attachment and the person who can answer questions about access. The background call history is retained in an internal record where it can be found if needed. The reader now encounters the information in the order required to act.
Use drafting assistance responsibly

A spelling aid, template, or AI-generated draft may suggest wording. You remain responsible for the claims, tone, permissions, and promises in the message. Check names, dates, quotations, and any statement that implies knowledge you do not possess. Remove invented examples or label them clearly. Do not send sensitive personal information to a service without appropriate permission and a suitable basis for using it.

Read the final version aloud. Does it sound like a responsible message you can explain? A polished sentence can still contain a false claim or an impossible commitment. The purpose of assistance is to help you communicate what is true and useful, rather than to create an impressive voice detached from your actual responsibility.
Visual summary
State the purpose early
Include essential context
Make the next action clear
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Perform a reader's review

Before sending, check the purpose, current facts, requested action, timing, attachment, audience, and privacy. Ask whether the reader can identify the next step without another explanation. If the stakes justify it, have a suitable person review the message. Keep the version actually sent where it belongs. If an error is discovered later, correct it with the people affected.
Prayer. Father, help my written words remain clear and truthful. Give me care for the reader, restraint about unnecessary detail, and responsibility for every claim and promise I send. Amen.
Chapter 8 Correct the Record and Keep Learning
Correct an inaccurate account with the people who received it.
Read Matthew 12:33–37, Proverbs 28:13, and Job 42:1–9.
Take responsibility for the words you used
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. — Proverbs 28:13, KJV

The proverb joins confession with turning from the wrong. If your words harmed someone, begin by identifying what you actually said or wrote. Do not make the apology depend on proving that you had a good intention. The hearer may need the inaccurate claim corrected, private information protected, or an arrangement changed so the conduct does not continue.

A clear acknowledgment names the deed and its effect. “I repeated an account I had not checked, and it wrongly placed blame on you” gives the other person an intelligible account. “I am sorry if anyone felt uncomfortable” may leave the conduct hidden. Keep the apology proportionate and avoid making the recipient responsible for reassuring you about your character.
Biblical testimony · Job's friends are corrected

Read Job 42:7–9 in the context of the whole book. The Lord addresses the friends concerning what they have said about Him, and the account gives a response they are to make. Their confident speeches did not become true merely because they sounded religious. The narrative challenges the temptation to give an explanation of another person's suffering that exceeds what God has revealed.

A modern speaker may need to admit, “I did not know why that happened and should not have claimed that I did.” You can still offer prayer, practical support, and truths about God's character grounded in Scripture. Correcting an unwarranted explanation can give a suffering person room to speak without carrying the added burden of your certainty.
Match the correction to the audience

If one person heard the error, contact that person appropriately. If a group received a false statement, the group may need the correction. If sensitive information was exposed, seek advice about limiting further harm before repeating it again in a supposedly corrective message. State enough for the audience to understand the correction without adding another unnecessary disclosure.

A correction should be discoverable beside the original where possible and appropriate. Do not quietly alter an important statement while leaving people dependent on the earlier version. Identify the change, its practical consequence, and any action now required. The aim is to restore an accurate shared account.
A worked correction after a meeting

Imagine a fictional manager in Edinburgh who says during a meeting that a volunteer failed to submit the figures. Later she discovers that the figures were sent to her and she overlooked the message. She tells the same group that the failure was hers, confirms that the volunteer submitted the work, and corrects the record used for planning.

She also apologizes directly to the volunteer and revises the process for checking submissions before making a public claim. The volunteer may still feel hurt, and the manager does not demand immediate reassurance. Her next conduct must support the correction. A practical change to the process makes the apology more than a request to stop discussing the event.
Build a review that teaches

Matthew 12:33–37 treats words seriously in relation to the heart and accountability before God. Read it with attention to Jesus' context. The passage should lead us toward repentance and truthful speech, rather than toward fearful examination of every accidental hesitation. Ask what your repeated messages reveal about a motive that needs attention.

Choose one recent exchange and review purpose, accuracy, clarity, manner, audience, and follow-through. Record one strength and one change. Ask a trusted person for feedback where it would help. Receive a correction about your message without immediately constructing a defense. Then practice the particular improvement in the next suitable situation.
Visual summary
Own the inaccurate statement
Correct the account directly

Continue with a thirty-day communication practice

Choose two purposes to work on, such as clearer requests and more accurate corrections. Prepare a brief message, use it in an appropriate real situation, and review its effect. Keep private details secure and alter identifying information when discussing an example with a mentor. At the end of the month, identify what improved and what still needs instruction.

Return to Ephesians 4:29 and ask whether your words served the hearer. A useful answer includes truth and practical effect. Continue with the next faithful message, allowing Scripture, responsible feedback, and the needs of real people to shape the words you choose.
Prayer. Lord, help me own the harm my words have caused and make a truthful correction. Teach me to keep learning and to speak and write with integrity, courage, and love. Amen.
